title: 2 Chronicles 19:1–11
context: 2 Chronicles 19:1–11 has no parallel in Kings. Jehoshaphat returns safely to Jerusalem, and Jehu the son of Hanani the seer rebukes him for helping the wicked and loving those who hate the LORD, while commending the good found in him. A Jehu son of Hanani also prophesies against Baasha of Israel in 1 Kings 16:1, 7, and a Hanani the seer rebukes Asa in 2 Chronicles 16:7; 20:34 later cites a history written by Jehu the son of Hanani. Whether these notices all refer to the same Jehu, and how the span of years fits, is discussed by interpreters and left open here. Kings records only that “Jehoshaphat made peace with the king of Israel.” (1 Kings 22:44), without a rebuke. Jehoshaphat then goes out among the people from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim to bring them back to the LORD and appoints judges in the fortified cities and a court in Jerusalem, with Amariah the chief priest over matters of the LORD and Zebadiah over the king’s matters. His charge echoes the law’s call for impartial justice (Deuteronomy 1:17; 16:18–20; 17:8–9). Both traditions read the chapter as shared ground: God disciplines and still commends his servant, and justice is administered as service to the LORD.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat the king of Judah returned to his house in peace to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat the king of Judah returns to his house in Jerusalem in peace. He returns as Ahab did not.

Arminian readers see God’s mercy in preserving a king who had walked into danger by his own choice, and they note that the safe return is a gift that calls for reflection and renewed faithfulness rather than complacency.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the contrast with Micaiah’s word to Ahab, who would not return in peace (18:27), and they see the LORD’s preserving care for the Davidic king even in the midst of his failure.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: Jehoshaphat’s safe return is a mercy, and the next verses show that mercy does not mean the alliance was approved.

verses.text: Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him, and said to King Jehoshaphat, “Should you help the wicked, and love those who hate the LORD? Because of this, wrath is on you from before the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehu the son of Hanani the seer meets him and asks, “Should you help the wicked, and love those who hate the LORD?” and declares that wrath is on him from the LORD because of this. Kings records no such rebuke.

Arminian readers note that the rebuke addresses a real, responsible choice, and they see God’s discipline as a call to repentance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God disciplining a king he loves, and they note that the rebuke names the alliance with Ahab as the problem. The Jehu son of Hanani of 1 Kings 16:1, 7, and the Hanani of 2 Chronicles 16:7, raise questions of identity and chronology that are left open.

Both traditions read the verse as a sober warning about partnership with those who oppose the LORD.

verses.text: Nevertheless there are good things found in you, in that you have put away the Asheroth out of the land, and have set your heart to seek God.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehu adds that good things are found in Jehoshaphat, because he has put away the Asheroth from the land and set his heart to seek God. Rebuke and commendation stand together.

Arminian readers note that God recognizes and honors genuine faithfulness even in a flawed servant, and they see the commendation as encouragement to continue seeking God after a failure.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s grace in naming the good he himself has worked in the king, and they note that the phrase about setting the heart to seek God sums up Chronicles’ picture of a faithful king.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and as a pastoral model: honest correction can be joined to real encouragement.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat lived at Jerusalem; and he went out again among the people from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim, and brought them back to the LORD, the God of their fathers.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat lives in Jerusalem and goes out again among the people from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim, bringing them back to the LORD, the God of their fathers. He responds to the rebuke with renewed reform.

Arminian readers see a king who takes correction to heart and works to call the people to return, a genuine response that God uses for the nation’s good.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that bringing the people back to the LORD is presented as the king’s work, yet the return of hearts is finally God’s work, and they see the king serving as God’s instrument of renewal.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about repentance expressed in renewed service and in care for the people’s faithfulness.

verses.text: He set judges in the land throughout all the fortified cities of Judah, city by city,
verses.arminianNotes:
He sets judges in the land throughout all the fortified cities of Judah, city by city. Justice is organized locally.

Arminian readers see a practical reform that brings justice within reach of ordinary people, and they note that faithful leaders work to make right judgment available in every community, not only in the capital.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the appointment of judges in the cities echoes the law’s command to appoint judges and officers in all the gates (Deuteronomy 16:18), and they see the reform as obedience to God’s word for the ordering of society.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about justice as part of covenant faithfulness.

verses.text: and said to the judges, “Consider what you do, for you don’t judge for man, but for the LORD; and he is with you in the judgment.
verses.arminianNotes:
He tells the judges to consider what they do, “for you don’t judge for man, but for the LORD; and he is with you in the judgment”.

Arminian readers note the weight of responsibility placed on each judge, who must choose to act justly as one accountable to God, and they see the promise that God is with them as real help in a demanding task.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that judgment belongs to God (compare Deuteronomy 1:17, “for the judgment is God’s”), so that human judges act as his servants, and they see this as the ground of both their authority and their accountability.

Both traditions read the charge as shared ground about justice done before the LORD.

verses.text: Now therefore let the fear of the LORD be on you. Take heed and do it; for there is no iniquity with the LORD our God, nor respect of persons, nor taking of bribes.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He urges them to let the fear of the LORD be on them, because there is no iniquity with the LORD, nor respect of persons, nor taking of bribes. The character of God is the standard for human judges.

Arminian readers note that the call to imitate God’s impartiality assumes judges can and must resist corruption.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see in the verse a clear statement of God’s own justice, and they note that it echoes the law’s prohibition, “You shall not take a bribe” (Deuteronomy 16:19), grounding human justice in divine character.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: those who judge must reflect the impartial justice of the God they serve, without favoritism or bribery.

verses.text: Moreover in Jerusalem Jehoshaphat appointed certain Levites, priests, and heads of the fathers’ households of Israel to give judgment for the LORD and for controversies. They returned to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
In Jerusalem Jehoshaphat appoints Levites, priests, and heads of the fathers’ households to give judgment for the LORD and for controversies. A central court is established.

Arminian readers see a careful arrangement that provides a place for difficult cases, and they note that faithful leadership includes building structures that help people receive justice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the arrangement resembles the law’s provision for hard cases to be brought to the priests who are Levites and to the judge at the place the LORD chooses (Deuteronomy 17:8–9). The final words, about returning to Jerusalem, are read in different ways.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about ordered justice.

verses.text: He commanded them, saying, “You shall do this in the fear of the LORD, faithfully, and with a perfect heart.
verses.arminianNotes:
He commands them to act in the fear of the LORD, faithfully, and with a perfect heart. Integrity is required of the court.

Arminian readers note the call to wholehearted faithfulness, and they see each member of the court as personally responsible to serve with integrity, a calling that requires daily choices to remain faithful under pressure.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the perfect heart in Chronicles describes undivided loyalty to God rather than sinless perfection, and they see the fear of the LORD as the root from which faithful service grows.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about integrity in those who serve the LORD in public office.

verses.text: Whenever any controversy comes to you from your brothers who dwell in their cities, between blood and blood, between law and commandment, statutes and ordinances, you must warn them, that they not be guilty toward the LORD, and so wrath come on you and on your brothers. Do this, and you will not be guilty.
verses.arminianNotes:
In every controversy brought from the cities, whether of bloodshed or of law, commandment, statutes, and ordinances, they must warn the people so that they do not become guilty before the LORD and bring wrath on themselves and their brothers.

Arminian readers see the judges’ duty to warn as a means by which people can turn from wrongdoing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the verse links justice with the covenant community’s standing before God, and they see the judges’ warnings as part of God’s appointed means for restraining sin and preserving his people from wrath.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: just judgment protects the community, and those who judge are accountable for faithful warning.

verses.text: Behold, Amariah the chief priest is over you in all matters of the LORD; and Zebadiah the son of Ishmael, the ruler of the house of Judah, in all the king’s matters. Also the Levites shall be officers before you. Deal courageously, and may the LORD be with the good.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Amariah the chief priest is over them in all matters of the LORD, and Zebadiah son of Ishmael, the ruler of the house of Judah, in all the king’s matters, with the Levites as officers; Jehoshaphat ends with, “Deal courageously, and may the LORD be with the good.”

Arminian readers see clear lines of responsibility and a call to courageous action.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the distinction between matters of the LORD and the king’s matters, and they see an ordered structure in which different leaders serve God in different spheres, though they caution against reading a modern theory of church and state into the verse.

Both traditions read the closing charge as shared ground about courage and justice under the LORD.
